synopsis: Unnecessary braking is the dominant documented automatic-braking failure mode in the cited on-road evidence, while nuisance interventions, production loss and operator disabling are repeatedly identified as reasons deployed mining proximity systems failed [f115, f1223, f116, f6306]. The on-road evidence includes an April 2024 NHTSA investigation covering 2,997,604 Honda vehicles; mining interviews found unnecessary vehicle shutdowns ranging from once a day to 15 times during a single cut of coal [f10422, f3285]. False braking is itself a safety hazard, potentially causing load shift, rollover, instability near edges or rear-end impacts, so validation must address machine-stability consequences as well as collision avoidance [f8201, f9370]. Acceptance should report nuisance and missed-intervention rates together, but the research found no published off-road hourly acceptance values; MOSH requires no false interventions or false warnings at its TRL4 gate, and conservative fail-to-safe intervention remains in tension with productivity and adoption [f6418, f2121, f2119, f5781]. Under a zero-event Poisson calculation, 300 representative hours without unnecessary braking support a 95% upper bound below one event per 100 hours, and 3,000 hours support below one per 1,000 hours, although the field exposure needed to substantiate rare unintended-braking probabilities remains uncertain [f6658, f6659, f8181]. Shadow mode can measure hypothetical nuisance interventions at scale but cannot establish consequences such as a following-truck collision, while simulators cannot establish long-term operator responses; validation should cover benign clutter and legitimate close approaches, with field monitoring after limited-domain release [f589, f596, f580, f8206, f4362, f3342, f722].
